analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurers to prove and publish that mental health coverage matches physical health coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees and two subcommittees, never received a vote, and died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law already says health plans must cover mental health and substance use care on equal terms with physical care, but insurers apply hidden limits like preauthorization and step therapy that are hard to check. This bill would have required insurers and employer plans to disclose the analyses they use to show compliance, subjected them to random audits with results posted publicly, set up a one-stop consumer complaint website, and required yearly public reporting of how often claims for mental health and addiction care are denied compared with other medical claims.
analysis.who_benefits: People with mental health or substance use disorders whose care is limited or denied by their insurance — including people denied residential treatment, therapy visits, or addiction medication. Also behavioral health providers who lose patients when coverage is denied.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People needing mental health or addiction care

how_it_helps.text: Requires group health plans and insurers to file annual reports disclosing the specific factors, evidence standards, and findings behind limits such as tiered benefits, step therapy, and preauthorization on mental health and substance use benefits, so regulators and consumers can see whether those limits are applied more harshly than to physical care [S2][S3].

Directs HHS, Labor, and Treasury to audit at least 12 plans per year for parity compliance, publish audit results, and publicly report the rates of and reasons for denying mental health and substance use claims compared with medical and surgical claims [S2][S3].

Creates a Consumer Parity Portal website where consumers can submit parity complaints that are routed to the right enforcement agency, and requires a GAO report on how well the departments actually enforce parity [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employer-sponsored group health plans bear the compliance cost of annual parity analyses, disclosures, and audits; the bill authorizes $2 million per year in federal spending for fiscal 2016-2020, and insurers may pass compliance costs into premiums.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employer health plans

drawbacks.text: Annual disclosure and audit requirements impose real compliance costs on insurers and employers who sponsor plans, which could flow into premiums [S3].
The bill authorizes $2 million per year for fiscal years 2016 through 2020 in new federal spending for enforcement, audits, and the consumer portal [S3].

Transparency alone does not force insurers to change behavior — the bill relies on published audit findings and complaint-driven enforcement rather than automatic penalties, so plans could stay technically compliant while contesting findings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly one in five adults affected by mental illness or substance use disorder, enforceable parity can mean the difference between covered treatment and out-of-pocket denial. The compliance costs are modest relative to the size of the group health insurance market, and the $2 million annual authorization is small. The main design weakness is that the bill creates transparency and complaint channels but no automatic penalty for plans found out of compliance; its teeth depend on regulators acting on what audits reveal.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees and then to two subcommittees, never received a markup or a floor vote, and died when the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Joseph Kennedy III introduced the bill on December 16, 2015, joined by Reps. Tonko, Matsui, Clarke, and Castor as original cosponsors, and it gathered 11 Democratic cosponsors in total [S3][S4].
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce, Education and the Workforce, and Ways and Means committees on the day of introduction [S1][S5].

Within days it was sent to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, and in March 2016 also to the Education and the Workforce's Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions Subcommittee; no committee or subcommittee ever voted on it [S5].
No further action was taken before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, so the bill never reached the House floor or the Senate [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer group health plans are better off because they never had to disclose their parity analyses, submit to annual public audits, or publish mental health denial rates. People whose mental health or addiction treatment gets quietly limited by preauthorization and step therapy are no better off than before.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 11 cosponsors were House Democrats, with no Republican support on record; no roll-call vote was ever taken.

industries.note: Insurers would have to disclose the inner workings of preauthorization, step therapy, and tiering decisions on mental health claims, undergo annual public audits, and have their denial rates published against medical and surgical denial rates. These are exactly the practices through which insurers limit expensive behavioral health care, so their business interest ran against the bill's purpose.

Self-insured employer plans governed by ERISA would bear new annual analysis and disclosure obligations, though employers whose plans already comply with parity would gain a clearer paper trail and employees would gain transparency.

industries.industry: Mental health and addiction treatment providers
industries.note: Stronger parity enforcement and public denial-rate data would reduce coverage denials that keep patients out of therapy, residential treatment, and addiction medication, directly increasing demand for these providers' services.
